style: very brief; three to six words per field, no detail unless asked

situations.name: Bedtime in her own room with the lights off
situations.feared_outcome: Someone is hiding in my closet and will come out when it's dark

behaviors.text: Needs the hall light on and her door wide open
Calls out 'are you still there?' to dad again and again after lights out
Gets out of bed after lights out and goes to sleep in her parents' bed

accommodations.text: Dad answers every 'are you still there?' call
Parents let her finish the night in their bed

situations.name: Going down to the basement playroom alone

behaviors.text: Won't go down to get her toys; asks someone else to fetch them
Sings very loudly on the basement stairs (could be play, could be to feel braver)

accommodations.text: Dad goes down and brings the toys up for her

situations.name: The power going out during a thunderstorm
situations.feared_outcome: The lights will never come back on

behaviors.text: Holds onto mom's arm and won't let go until the lights come back

monitoring_log.child_behavior_observed: Wouldn't go down for her dolls.
Glued to mom's arm till lights back.
Went halfway down singing really loud. Came back up.
Told her I'd check closet. Checked closet.
monitoring_log.trap: parent action written in child field (dad checking the closet is his action, not Pearl's)

monitoring_log.parent_words: bedtime again. light on. came to our room midnight. walked her back.

voice_notes.text: lucia bedtime um light on door open she called out like are you there maybe six times I said yes every time she said seven
voice_notes.trap: 'six times' is a count of calls, not a fear level; the fear level is 7

turns.text: Okay, let's get started. Pearl, I love your sparkly shoes. Dad, thanks for the log this week. It was short, but it had what I needed, so don't worry about writing more. I want to go through it with both of you. Is that okay, Pearl?
Okay.
So the biggest thing in here is bedtime. It looks like most nights the hall light is on and your door is open, and you call out to Dad a lot. Can you tell me what bedtime is like for you?
It's dark and the closet is dark too. And sometimes the closet door is a little bit open.
And when the closet door is a little bit open in the dark, what does your worry tell you?
That somebody is in there. Hiding. And they come out when it's all the way dark.
That sounds really scary to think about when you're trying to fall asleep. Has anybody ever come out of your closet?
No. Just my coats are in there.
Just your coats. So your worry is telling you something big, and what's actually in there is coats. Dad, what happens on your end at bedtime?

Light stays on in the hall. Door open. Then she calls out, are you there, are you there. I say yes. Some nights it's five or six times, some nights more. Then usually around midnight or two she's in our bed.
And you let her stay?
Usually. We're tired. One night I walked her back. It took forever.

That's honest, thank you. Being tired at two in the morning is real. I want to explain what I think is happening, and then we'll make a plan that doesn't ask too much at once. Each time Pearl calls out and you answer, she gets a little bit of relief. Each time she comes to your bed and stays, she gets a lot of relief. Her brain learns that the only way to be safe in the dark is to have you close. So the dark never gets a chance to feel normal. Does that make sense?
Yes. Makes sense.
Pearl, let's do the thermometer. Zero means not scared at all, ten means the most scared ever. Bedtime with the hall light on and your door open. What number?
Seven.
Seven. And bedtime with the hall light off?
Ten. No, nine.
Okay, nine. Thanks for thinking about it. Now Dad also wrote about the storm. The power went out?
Last Friday. Power was out about forty minutes. She held onto her mom's arm the whole time. Her mom lit candles.
I thought the lights were never coming back. Ever.
That would be a big scary thought. And they did come back, right?
Yeah. The fridge made a noise and then they came back.
So that's one we won't practice on purpose, because we can't make a storm happen. But it's good to know about. Now, the basement. Dad, you wrote she won't go down for her toys.
Right. I go get them. And Sunday she went halfway down singing really loud and came back up.
Pearl, tell me about the singing. I'm curious about it.
It's a song from school. About a frog.
Do you sing it on the stairs because it's fun, or because it helps you feel less scared, or something else?
I don't know. I just sing it.

That's an okay answer. We don't have to know yet. Dad, I'd like you to just notice when she sings, whether it's on the stairs or other places too. We'll figure out what it's for later. And what number is the basement, Pearl? Going down there by yourself?
I don't know.

That's fine, you can think about it this week. So here's what I'd like to try. We're going to start with bedtime, because it happens every night and that gives us lots of practice. Pearl, I don't want to turn off the hall light yet. That's a nine, that's too big. What I want to change first is the calling out.
But I need to know Dad is there.

I understand. So here's the deal. Dad is going to give you three tickets. They're little paper tickets. Each time you call out, are you there, you use one ticket, and Dad answers. When the tickets are used up, Dad doesn't answer, but he's still right there in the house. And if you have any tickets left in the morning, you can trade them for something. Dad, what would be a good trade?
Pancakes on a school day. She'd do a lot for pancakes.
Chocolate chip pancakes.

Chocolate chip pancakes it is. And Dad, the second part is for you. If she comes to your bed in the night, you walk her back to her own bed. Calm, boring, not much talking. You can sit with her for a minute, but you don't stay. I know it took forever the one night you did it. It usually gets faster after a few nights. Can you two try that this week?
Yes. Three tickets, no answer after that. Walk her back.
And keep writing it down, short is fine. Write how many tickets she used and whether she came to your bed. Pearl, what number do you think the tickets would be?
Five. If I have the tickets I'm okay.

Five sounds like a good brave step. Not too easy, not too hard. Okay, I think we have our plan. Tickets, walking back to bed, and Dad notices the singing. I'll see you both next week. Bring me a ticket if you have one left.
Okay. Bye.
